questions.question: When is few-shot prompting the right tool?

options.A: When the model needs more factual knowledge
options.C: When output format or edge-case handling is inconsistent and examples can demonstrate the target behavior
options.B: When latency must be reduced
options.D: When the context window is too small

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples fix format and edge-case behavior far better than more instructions

questions.question: A page retrieved by your agent contains hidden text instructing it to reveal its system prompt. Which mitigation actually works?

options.A: Asking the model in the system prompt to ignore such instructions
options.D: Treating retrieved content as untrusted data, separating it from instructions, and gating sensitive capabilities behind guardrails
options.B: Raising temperature so behavior is less predictable
options.C: Filtering pages that contain the word "ignore"

questions.rationale: Injection defense is structural: separate untrusted content and apply least privilege to consequential tools

questions.question: Which statement about the Message Batches API is correct?

options.B: It supports multi-turn tool calling within a batch
options.A: It processes large asynchronous workloads at reduced cost within a processing window, correlating requests by custom_id
options.C: It guarantees sub-second latency
options.D: It requires a dedicated endpoint per request

questions.rationale: Reduced cost, asynchronous window, custom_id correlation, and no multi-turn tool calling inside a batch

questions.question: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively and must parse its output. Which invocation fits?

options.A: Interactive mode with output piped to a file
options.B: The print flag with a JSON output format and a schema, so results are machine-readable and validated
options.C: Plan mode with a human approver
options.D: A wrapper that screen-scrapes the terminal

questions.rationale: Headless CI use means non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.question: Traces show your assistant reasons correctly over the documents it receives, but frequently receives documents unrelated to the question. Where is the defect?

options.A: The model, which should be upgraded
options.C: The retrieval layer that selects the documents
options.B: The system prompt, which needs stronger accuracy language
options.D: The output parser

questions.rationale: Traces localize the fault to the integration layer: correct reasoning over wrong inputs is a retrieval defect

questions.question: A service sends the same 8,000-token system prompt on every request and cost is dominated by input tokens. What is the first change to evaluate?

options.A: Rewriting the system prompt to be shorter
options.B: Switching to a cheaper model
options.C: Caching the stable prefix so it is not reprocessed on every call
options.D: Reducing the number of requests

questions.rationale: A large unchanging prefix repeated per call is what caching addresses, without losing any instruction. Shortening (A) sacrifices capability, a cheaper model (B) trades quality, and fewer requests (D) changes the product

questions.question: An endpoint must return within 500 ms but the model needs longer for a good answer. What is the appropriate pattern?

options.A: Return an acknowledgement immediately and deliver the result through a callback or poll
options.B: Truncate the model's output
options.C: Use the smallest model regardless of quality
options.D: Increase the timeout on the client

questions.rationale: Decoupling acceptance from completion satisfies the latency contract without degrading the answer. Truncation (B) and a minimal model (C) sacrifice the result, and the timeout (D) is the stated constraint

questions.question: What does a stop reason indicating the maximum token limit tell you?

options.A: The input was too long
options.B: The request was malformed
options.C: The model refused the request
options.D: The output was cut off before the model finished

questions.rationale: That stop reason reports that generation hit the output ceiling. An oversized input (A) fails before generation, and neither a malformed request (B) nor a refusal (C) produces this reason

questions.question: A tool result returns 50,000 tokens of JSON, most of it unused. What is the right fix?

options.A: Raise the model's context limit
options.B: Change the tool to return only the fields the task needs
options.C: Summarise the JSON with a second model call
options.D: Call the tool less frequently

questions.rationale: Tools should return what the task requires, which preserves context for reasoning. A larger window (A) delays the problem, a second call (C) adds cost and failure surface, and calling less often (D) does not change the payload

questions.question: Which condition warrants a retry with backoff rather than surfacing an error?

options.A: The request contained an invalid parameter
options.B: The service returned a rate limit or a transient server error
options.C: The model returned an answer you disagree with
options.D: The response exceeded the expected length

questions.rationale: Rate limits and transient server errors are the recoverable class. An invalid parameter (A) will fail identically, and disagreement (C) or length (D) are not transport failures

questions.question: A workload runs nightly over 50,000 records with no interactive requirement. Which choice reduces cost most?

options.A: Streaming each request
options.B: Using the largest model for accuracy
options.C: Increasing concurrency against the standard endpoint
options.D: Submitting the work as a batch

questions.rationale: Large, uniform, latency-tolerant work is exactly the batch case, and it is materially cheaper. Streaming (A) serves interactive use, the largest model (B) raises cost, and concurrency (C) does not change unit price

questions.question: Accuracy on a simple extraction task is identical between a small and a large model. What should be deployed?

options.A: The small model, since it meets the requirement at lower cost
options.B: The large model, in case inputs change
options.C: Both, alternating between them
options.D: The newest model available

questions.rationale: Where the requirement is met, the cheaper option is correct, and changing inputs are handled by re-evaluating. Insurance against hypothetical change (B), alternation (C), and recency (D) all spend without benefit

questions.question: A task requires the model to plan across many interacting constraints and revise as it goes. What does this argue for?

options.A: The smallest model, to keep cost down
options.B: Splitting the task across several small models
options.C: A more capable model, since the work is reasoning-heavy
options.D: A longer prompt with the same model

questions.rationale: Multi-step reasoning under interacting constraints is where capability differences show. A small model (A) and splitting (B) both fragment the reasoning, and prompt length (D) does not add capability

questions.question: An agent is given ten tools, three of which overlap in purpose. What is the likely consequence?

options.A: Faster execution, since more options are available
options.B: Lower token cost
options.C: Better error handling
options.D: More frequent wrong tool selection

questions.rationale: Overlapping tools make selection ambiguous, which is where agents go wrong. Overlap does not improve speed (A), reduce cost (B), or help error handling (C)

questions.question: What should terminate an agent loop?

options.A: A fixed wall-clock timeout only
options.B: The model deciding it is finished
options.C: An explicit success condition, with a step ceiling as a backstop
options.D: Running out of context

questions.rationale: A defined success condition ends the loop correctly, and the ceiling bounds the failure case. A timeout alone (A) does not recognise success, the model's own judgment (B) is not a guarantee, and exhausting context (D) is a failure rather than a termination

questions.question: Where should a stable instruction that must apply to every turn be placed?

options.A: At the end of the latest user message
options.B: In the system prompt
options.C: Repeated in each user message
options.D: In a tool description

questions.rationale: The system prompt is designed for persistent framing across the exchange. Placing it in user turns (A, C) mixes configuration with input, and tool descriptions (D) govern tool selection

questions.question: Which change most improves output that is correct but inconsistently formatted?

options.A: Providing an example of the exact output required
options.B: Raising the temperature
options.C: Asking for the output to be neat
options.D: Using a larger model

questions.rationale: An example defines the target unambiguously, which is what formatting consistency needs. Higher temperature (B) increases variance, a vague adjective (C) does not specify, and a larger model (D) does not know your format

questions.question: What is the most important property of a tool description?

options.A: It states what the tool does, when to use it, and what each parameter means
options.B: It is short
options.C: It lists the implementation language
options.D: It matches the function name exactly

questions.rationale: The description is the model's only basis for choosing and calling the tool correctly. Brevity (B) is secondary to clarity, and implementation detail (C) and naming (D) do not guide selection

questions.question: Content retrieved from an external site contains instructions aimed at the model. What is the correct defence?

options.A: Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore such content
options.B: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data and bound the model's permissions outside the prompt
options.C: Scan for known injection phrases and block them
options.D: Use a model with a larger context window

questions.rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its granted permissions regardless of what the content says. Prompt instructions (A) and phrase filters (C) are bypassable, and context size (D) is irrelevant

questions.question: A prompt change improved results on the five examples you tested. What should happen before it reaches production?

options.A: Ship it, since all five improved
options.B: Ask the model to compare the two prompts
options.C: Evaluate it against a held-out set that reflects real inputs, on defined criteria
options.D: Ship it to a small percentage of traffic and watch error rates

questions.rationale: Five hand-picked cases cannot separate a real gain from noise, which is what an evaluation set settles. Self-comparison (B) is not measurement, and shipping first (A, D) makes users the test

questions.question: A request fails with an authentication error after working for months. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A transient service fault
options.B: The prompt became too long
options.C: A credential that expired, was rotated, or lost its permissions
options.D: The model was deprecated

questions.rationale: Authentication failures point at the credential rather than the payload. A transient fault (A) presents differently, and neither prompt length (B) nor deprecation (D) produces an auth error

questions.question: What is the purpose of correlating a request identifier through an integration?

options.A: It lets a specific response be traced back to the request that produced it
options.B: It reduces token cost
options.C: It improves model accuracy
options.D: It is required by the API

questions.rationale: Correlation exists for traceability, which is what debugging asynchronous or batched work depends on. It does not affect cost (B) or accuracy (C), and it is a design practice rather than a requirement (D)

questions.question: An integration must handle a response that stops early because the model called a tool. What does the application do next?

options.A: Treat it as an error and retry
options.B: Return the partial text to the user
options.C: Increase the output token limit
options.D: Execute the tool and return its result so the model can continue

questions.rationale: A tool-use stop is a handoff, and the loop continues once the result is returned. Retrying (A) repeats the request, returning partial text (B) discards the work, and the token limit (C) is unrelated

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason to put a queue between an application and the model?

options.A: It makes responses more accurate
options.B: It absorbs bursts so load stays within rate limits without dropping work
options.C: It reduces the token count
options.D: It removes the need for retries

questions.rationale: A queue smooths demand against a rate-limited dependency. It does not change accuracy (A) or token counts (C), and retries remain necessary (D)

questions.question: A response arrives well-formed but semantically wrong for the input. Where should investigation start?

options.A: The transport layer
options.B: The prompt and the exact context supplied for that input
options.C: The rate limit configuration
options.D: The output token limit

questions.rationale: A well-formed but wrong answer points at what the model was told, not how it was delivered. Transport (A), limits (C), and output caps (D) produce failures of delivery rather than of meaning

questions.question: What is the practical consequence of choosing a model with a much larger context window than the task needs?

options.A: Better accuracy on every task
options.B: Fewer rate limit errors
options.C: More reliable structured output
options.D: Cost and latency that the task does not require

questions.rationale: Unused capacity is paid for in cost and time. A larger window does not itself improve accuracy (A), reduce rate limiting (B), or make structure more reliable (C)

questions.question: How should a team decide when to move a task to a smaller model?

options.A: When measurement shows the smaller model meets the task's stated quality bar
options.B: When the budget is exceeded
options.C: When the task becomes high volume
options.D: When latency becomes a complaint

questions.rationale: The decision is evidence-led against a defined bar. Budget (B), volume (C), and latency (D) create pressure to look, but they do not establish that quality holds

questions.question: A long-running agent needs to keep a decision it made twenty steps ago. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Rely on the context window retaining it
options.B: Increase the temperature
options.C: Write it into an explicit state that is carried forward regardless of compaction
options.D: Restart the agent periodically

questions.rationale: Durable state must be explicit, because context is finite and compaction is lossy. Relying on the window (A) fails at length, temperature (B) is unrelated, and restarting (D) loses the decision

questions.question: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in practice?

options.A: Workflows are shorter
options.B: Agents cannot use tools
options.C: Workflows cannot call the model
options.D: In a workflow the control flow is fixed in advance; in an agent the model chooses the next step

questions.rationale: Who decides the next step is the distinction that matters. Length (A) is incidental, agents do use tools (B), and workflows do call the model (C)

questions.question: A prompt contains an instruction that contradicts an example in the same prompt. What is the likely outcome?

options.A: The instruction always wins
options.B: The example always wins
options.C: Behaviour becomes unpredictable between the two
options.D: The request is rejected

questions.rationale: Contradictory signals produce inconsistent behaviour rather than a defined precedence. Neither the instruction (A) nor the example (B) reliably wins, and the request is not rejected (D)

questions.question: What is the effect of placing the most important instruction in the middle of a very long prompt?

options.A: None, position is irrelevant
options.B: It is more likely to be overlooked than if it were at a boundary
options.C: It is followed more closely
options.D: It causes an error

questions.rationale: Material at the edges of a long input is attended to more reliably than material buried in the middle. Position is not neutral (A) or advantageous here (C), and it does not error (D)

questions.question: When should a tool return an identifier rather than the full object?

options.A: When the object is large and the model only needs it to make a subsequent call
options.B: Never, the model needs the full object
options.C: Always, to reduce cost
options.D: Only for write operations

questions.rationale: Returning a handle keeps context free when the payload is only needed for a later call. Always returning everything (B) or nothing (C) ignores the task, and the rule is not about writes (D)

questions.question: An MCP server is added and the agent's success rate falls. What should be checked first?

options.A: Whether the new tools overlap with existing ones and have distinguishable descriptions
options.B: The server's uptime
options.C: The model version
options.D: The network latency

questions.rationale: A new tool surface most often degrades selection through overlap and unclear descriptions. Uptime (B) and latency (D) present as errors or slowness, and the model did not change (C)

questions.question: A model output will be rendered directly into a web page. What must the application do?

options.A: Nothing, model output is safe
options.B: Treat the output as untrusted and escape or sanitise it before rendering
options.C: Ask the model not to produce markup
options.D: Use a larger model

questions.rationale: Anything rendered into a page is escaped regardless of source, since output can be influenced by input. Assuming safety (A) and instructing the model (C) are not controls, and model size (D) is irrelevant

questions.question: What does a regression suite protect against that a one-off evaluation does not?

options.A: Slow responses
options.B: Rate limits
options.C: A change that improves the target behaviour while quietly breaking another
options.D: Cost increases

questions.rationale: Regressions are silent by definition and are caught by continuously testing what must not break. Latency (A), limits (B), and cost (D) are operational signals rather than correctness

questions.question: Your support agent resolves most tickets but sometimes loops indefinitely, re-calling lookup_order on the same order. What is the correct structural fix?

options.A: Raise max_tokens so the loop has room to finish
options.C: Add explicit loop-termination conditions: cap tool iterations, detect repeated identical calls, and route to escalate_to_human when progress stalls
options.B: Remove the lookup_order tool
options.D: Lower the temperature

questions.rationale: Agent loops need engineered termination: iteration budgets, repeated-call detection, and an escalation path when the agent cannot progress. Token budget (A) delays the symptom, removing a needed tool (B) breaks resolution, and temperature (D) does not bound iteration.

questions.question: process_refund currently accepts any amount. Support policy caps agent-initiated refunds at $200; larger refunds need a human. Where does that rule belong?

options.A: In the system prompt, phrased firmly
options.D: Enforced in the tool layer: the tool rejects amounts over the cap with a structured error, and a hook or the tool itself routes larger cases to escalation
options.B: In the model's reasoning, since it reads the policy
options.C: In quarterly staff training

questions.rationale: Hard policy limits are enforced deterministically at the tool boundary, not requested of the model. Prompt phrasing (A) and model reasoning (B) are probabilistic where the requirement is absolute, and training (C) does not constrain the agent at all.

questions.question: Your coordinator delegates to search, analysis, and report subagents. Final reports cite sources that do not support their claims, though each subagent behaves sensibly alone. What is the most likely architectural cause?

options.B: The report subagent's model is too small
options.A: Provenance is lost at handoffs: findings and their sources are not passed together in a structured form, so the report writer pairs claims with citations by guesswork
options.C: The web is unreliable
options.D: Too many subagents are running in parallel

questions.rationale: In multi-agent pipelines, provenance survives only if the handoff format carries claim and source together. That failure mode produces exactly this symptom while every stage looks locally fine. Model size (B), source quality (C), and parallelism (D) do not explain correct facts paired with wrong citations.

questions.question: The analysis subagent returns 30,000-token document dumps to the coordinator, which then fails on context limits. What is the right fix?

options.A: Give the coordinator a bigger context window
options.B: Have subagents return structured extracts, findings with citations and confidence, while full documents stay in the subagent's context or a scratchpad file
options.C: Have the coordinator drop the oldest messages silently
options.D: Run the analysis twice and keep the shorter answer

questions.rationale: Context isolation is the point of subagent delegation: raw bulk stays at the edge, distilled results travel. A larger window (A) postpones the failure, silent dropping (C) loses arbitrary information, and rerunning (D) changes nothing structural.

questions.question: Your monorepo has frontend and backend directories with different conventions, and one team-wide rule about commit style. Where does each piece of configuration belong?

options.A: Everything in one root CLAUDE.md
options.C: The commit rule in the project-level CLAUDE.md; the per-area conventions in path-scoped rules under .claude/rules/ that load only when matching files are touched
options.B: Each engineer's personal user-level CLAUDE.md
options.D: A wiki page linked from the README

questions.rationale: The hierarchy exists for exactly this: shared rules at project scope, conditional conventions path-scoped so context is spent only where relevant. One root file (A) loads everything everywhere, personal files (B) diverge per engineer, and a wiki (D) never reaches the model.

questions.question: Your CI job runs Claude Code to review pull requests, and the pipeline must parse the results mechanically. Which invocation is correct?

options.A: Interactive mode with a human copying the output into CI
options.D: Non-interactive mode with -p, with --output-format json and a schema so the review arrives as machine-readable, validated output
options.B: Plan mode, which is safer for automation
options.C: A shell script that greps the human-readable transcript

questions.rationale: Headless CI use is what -p with JSON output and a schema is for: deterministic invocation, parseable results. A human in the loop (A) is not CI, plan mode (B) is a review gate for interactive work rather than an output format, and grepping prose (C) breaks on the first wording change.

questions.domain: Claude Code in CI, Prompt Engineering
questions.question: The automated reviewer flags dozens of trivial style nits per pull request, and engineers have started ignoring it. Which change addresses the false-positive problem the way the blueprint suggests?

options.B: Run the review twice and post only findings that appear both times
options.A: Define explicit review criteria in the prompt: what to flag, what to ignore, and a severity bar, with a few worked examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
options.C: Cap the reviewer at three findings per pull request
options.D: Route all findings to a channel nobody reads

questions.rationale: Precision comes from explicit criteria and few-shot examples that draw the boundary between signal and noise. Double-running (B) filters randomness but not systematic nit-picking, an arbitrary cap (C) drops real findings on bad days, and (D) is surrender.

questions.question: Invoices sometimes lack a purchase-order number, and your extraction schema must handle that honestly while catching real misses. What is the right schema design?

options.A: Make every field required so nothing is missed
options.B: Make purchase_order nullable, so absence is recorded as null, and validate that it is present whenever the document type requires it
options.C: Make everything optional to avoid validation errors
options.D: Have the model invent a plausible number when one is missing

questions.rationale: Schema design encodes reality: genuinely optional data is nullable, and conditional requirements are validated downstream. All-required (A) forces fabrication or failure on legitimate documents, all-optional (C) blinds you to true misses, and invention (D) is data corruption.

questions.question: Your pipeline reports 98% field accuracy, measured on the documents the schema validated cleanly. An auditor calls the number misleading. Why?

options.A: Accuracy should be measured only on the hardest documents
options.C: Validation-clean documents are a biased sample: the honest measure comes from a labeled sample drawn across all documents, including ones that failed or barely passed validation
options.B: 98% is below industry standard
options.D: Field accuracy is not a real metric

questions.rationale: Measuring only where the system already succeeded inflates the estimate; calibration requires a labeled sample representative of the full input stream. Hardest-only (A) biases in the opposite direction, the standard claim (B) is invented, and (D) is false.

questions.question: Your codebase-exploration agent has get_file_contents, read_source, and fetch_file tools that all read files, and it frequently picks poorly among them. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Add a fourth, better file-reading tool
options.D: Consolidate to one file-reading tool, or give the survivors sharply differentiated descriptions that state exactly when each applies
options.B: Fine-tune the model on the tool list
options.C: Randomize which tool the harness dispatches

questions.rationale: Tool selection runs on descriptions; overlapping tools with vague descriptions produce dithering. Consolidation or sharp differentiation is the documented cure. Adding overlap (A) worsens it, fine-tuning (B) is disproportionate, and randomization (C) institutionalizes the confusion.

questions.question: A support workflow resolves tickets by looking up an account, checking entitlement, and drafting a reply, always in that order. Which architecture is correct?

options.B: A single agent that decides each step at runtime
options.A: A deterministic pipeline that calls the model at each defined step
options.C: Three agents that negotiate the order between them
options.D: One prompt containing all three steps

questions.rationale: A known, fixed sequence should be encoded rather than rediscovered on every run, which makes it cheaper, faster, and testable step by step. Runtime decisions (B, C) add nondeterminism for no gain, and one prompt (D) removes the checkpoints between steps.

questions.question: What is the strongest justification for splitting work across subagents?

options.A: The task has many steps
options.B: Separate lines of work each need their own context, and mixing them degrades both
options.C: Subagents are faster than a single agent
options.D: The output must be assembled from several sections

questions.rationale: Subagents exist to isolate context, so the case for them is contamination between concerns rather than volume. Step count (A) and sectioned output (D) suit a workflow, and delegation usually adds latency rather than removing it (C).

questions.question: An agent loops between two tools without converging. What is the most appropriate first control?

options.A: Increase the context window so it can see more history
options.C: Impose a step ceiling and define the terminating condition explicitly
options.B: Switch to a larger model
options.D: Remove one of the two tools

questions.rationale: Non-termination is bounded by an explicit stop condition and a hard ceiling, which contains cost and makes the failure visible. More context (A) and a larger model (B) do not guarantee convergence, and removing a tool (D) may break the task.

questions.question: Which property most increases the operational risk of an agentic design?

options.A: It calls more than one model
options.D: It takes irreversible actions without a checkpoint
options.B: It produces structured output
options.C: It runs longer than a minute

questions.rationale: Reversibility governs the cost of being wrong, which is the dominant risk in autonomous execution. Multiple models (A), structure (B), and duration (C) affect cost and complexity rather than blast radius.

questions.question: How should an agentic system handle a step whose result it cannot verify?

options.B: Proceed, since the model is usually right
options.A: Surface the unverifiable step for human confirmation before acting on it
options.C: Retry the step until two runs agree
options.D: Log the step and continue

questions.rationale: An unverifiable result is exactly where human judgment belongs, before it is acted upon. Assuming correctness (B) and logging without stopping (D) both act on unchecked output, and agreement across runs (C) establishes consistency rather than truth.

questions.question: A team proposes an agent for a task where every input is well formed and every rule is known. What should the architect recommend?

options.A: An agent, for future flexibility
options.B: A deterministic implementation, reserving model calls for the genuinely ambiguous parts
options.C: An agent with a low step limit
options.D: A multi-agent design for separation of concerns

questions.rationale: Known rules over well-formed input are code, and using a model there buys nondeterminism at a price. Speculative flexibility (A), a constrained agent (C), and multiple agents (D) all keep the cost without the need.

questions.question: What most improves the debuggability of an agentic system in production?

options.A: Reducing the number of tools
options.C: Recording the inputs, tool calls, and outputs of each step as a trace
options.B: Using a single model for every step
options.D: Increasing the step limit

questions.rationale: A per-step trace is what makes a nondeterministic run reconstructable after the fact. Fewer tools (A) and one model (B) simplify without explaining, and a higher ceiling (D) makes failures longer rather than clearer.

questions.question: Where should conventions that apply to everyone working in a repository be recorded?

options.A: In each developer's personal settings
options.D: In a CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
options.B: In the pull request template
options.C: In a pinned chat message

questions.rationale: Committed project memory is versioned, reviewable, and shared, which is what a team convention requires. Personal settings (A) do not propagate, and templates (B) and messages (C) are not read as working context.

questions.question: What distinguishes work suited to headless mode?

options.B: It is complex and needs close supervision
options.A: It is well defined and repeatable, so it can run unattended in automation
options.C: It requires many tools
options.D: It produces a long output

questions.rationale: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work where no one is watching. Supervision (B) argues for interactive use, and tool count (C) and output length (D) do not determine suitability.

questions.question: A skill and a subagent could both address a need. What decides between them?

options.A: Skills are always preferable
options.B: Whether the need is reusable know-how or an isolated line of work with its own context
options.C: Whether the task is long
options.D: Whether the repository already has a CLAUDE.md

questions.rationale: The two solve different problems: a skill packages reusable procedure, a subagent isolates context. A blanket preference (A), duration (C), and existing files (D) do not address that distinction.

questions.question: What is the correct use of a hook in a Claude Code workflow?

options.A: To hold instructions the model should follow
options.C: To enforce a deterministic action at a defined point, independently of the model
options.B: To store project context
options.D: To define which model is used

questions.rationale: Hooks run as code at fixed points, so they enforce rather than request. Instructions (A) and context (B) belong in project memory, and model choice (D) is configuration.

questions.question: Claude Code performs well for one engineer and inconsistently across the team. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The others need more capable machines
options.D: The working conventions live in one person's local setup rather than in the repository
options.B: The repository is too large
options.C: The others are using different terminals

questions.rationale: Context that is not committed does not travel, which produces exactly this asymmetry. Hardware (A), repository size (B), and terminal choice (C) do not explain a difference in output quality.

questions.question: A pipeline requires output that always validates against a schema. What is the correct approach?

options.B: Ask for the schema in the prompt and validate afterwards
options.A: Declare the schema as a tool the model must call, and validate on receipt
options.C: Ask for JSON and repair malformed output in code
options.D: Use a lower temperature

questions.rationale: A declared schema makes the structure part of the contract rather than a request, and validation on receipt closes the loop. Prompt requests (B), downstream repair (C), and temperature (D) all leave the shape to chance.

questions.question: Extraction is accurate for common cases and fails on rare formats. What is the most effective response?

options.A: Raise the temperature to encourage flexibility
options.B: Add examples covering the rare formats and define what to return when a field is absent
options.C: Switch to a larger model
options.D: Ask the model to try harder on unusual inputs

questions.rationale: Rare cases fail because they are unspecified, and examples plus an explicit absent-field rule specify them. Temperature (A) adds variance, a larger model (C) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (D) is not a specification.

questions.question: What should a schema define for a field the source document may not contain?

options.A: Nothing, since the model will omit it
options.C: An explicit representation for absence, so a missing value is distinguishable from an unfilled one
options.B: A default value that looks plausible
options.D: A free-text field for notes

questions.rationale: Absence must be representable, or downstream code cannot tell a genuine gap from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, plausible defaults (B) fabricate data, and a notes field (D) does not make the state machine-readable.

questions.question: Which practice most improves consistency across a long-running structured extraction job?

options.A: Randomising the order of documents
options.D: Fixing the prompt, the schema, and the model version, and recording them with the output
options.B: Increasing the output token limit
options.C: Running each document twice

questions.rationale: Consistency requires that the things that shape output are pinned and recorded, so results remain comparable and reproducible. Ordering (A) is irrelevant, the token cap (B) affects length, and duplicate runs (C) measure variance without removing it.

questions.question: A prompt mixes the instruction, the data, and the output format in continuous prose. What is the first improvement?

options.B: Shorten it
options.A: Separate the sections so the instruction, the input, and the required format are distinguishable
options.C: Move it into the system prompt
options.D: Add emphasis to the format requirement

questions.rationale: Structure lets the model tell instruction from data, which is the most common source of confusion in long prompts. Shortening (B) may remove needed detail, relocation (C) does not clarify, and emphasis (D) does not separate.

questions.question: What is the strongest indicator that a tool surface needs redesign?

options.A: It contains more than ten tools
options.B: The model regularly selects a tool that cannot accomplish the request
options.C: The tools return JSON
options.D: The tools are implemented across several services

questions.rationale: Repeated wrong selection is evidence that the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (A), return format (C), and implementation topology (D) are not themselves problems.

questions.question: How should a tool that performs an irreversible action be designed?

options.A: With a description warning the model to be careful
options.C: So that authorisation and confirmation are enforced outside the model
options.B: So that it requires more parameters
options.D: So that it is declared last

questions.rationale: Irreversibility is controlled by the surrounding system, because a prompt-level warning is a request rather than a guarantee. Extra parameters (B) and ordering (D) do not constrain authority.

questions.question: A tool returns a large payload that consumes most of the context window. What is the right change?

options.A: Increase the context window
options.D: Return only what the task needs, with a way to request more detail
options.B: Summarise the payload with a second model call
options.C: Call the tool less often

questions.rationale: Tools should return task-relevant results rather than everything available, which keeps context for reasoning. A larger window (A) postpones the problem, a second call (B) adds cost and a failure point, and calling less often (C) does not change the payload.

questions.question: What belongs in a tool's description?

options.B: The implementation language and framework
options.A: What the tool does, when to use it, and what its parameters mean
options.C: The service level agreement
options.D: The name of the team that owns it

questions.rationale: The description is the model's selection guide, so it must answer purpose, applicability, and parameters. Implementation detail (B), service levels (C), and ownership (D) are irrelevant to the choice.

questions.question: A long agentic run degrades in quality as it proceeds. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The model version changed mid-run
options.B: Context has accumulated until relevant material competes with stale material
options.C: The temperature was set too low
options.D: The tools became slower

questions.rationale: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation and drift. Versions do not change mid-run (A), low temperature (C) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: What is the right way to carry state across a compaction boundary?

options.A: Rely on the model to remember what mattered
options.C: Write the decisions and constraints that must persist into an explicit summary that is carried forward
options.B: Increase the context window so compaction is never needed
options.D: Restart the task after compaction

questions.rationale: Persistence must be deliberate, because compaction is lossy by design. Relying on recall (A) is unreliable, a larger window (B) only delays the boundary, and restarting (D) discards the work.

questions.question: Which measure most improves reliability for a workflow that must not silently produce wrong output?

options.A: A larger model
options.D: A validation step that can reject output and trigger a defined fallback
options.B: A longer prompt
options.C: More examples in the prompt

questions.rationale: Reliability against silent failure requires detection and a defined response, which is what validation with a fallback provides. Model size (A), prompt length (B), and examples (C) improve the average case without catching the bad one.

questions.question: What should be measured to know whether a production agentic system is healthy?

options.B: Total tokens consumed
options.A: Task success against a defined criterion, plus the rate and shape of failures
options.C: Average response time
options.D: The number of tool calls per run

questions.rationale: Health is defined by whether the system accomplishes the task and how it fails when it does not. Tokens (B), latency (C), and call counts (D) are cost and behaviour signals that say nothing about correctness.

questions.question: The agent occasionally answers billing questions using an order it looked up three turns earlier for a different customer. What is the architectural fix?

options.A: Increase the context window
options.B: Scope each conversation's context to one customer and clear or isolate prior lookups when the subject changes
options.C: Remove the lookup_order tool
options.D: Instruct the model to be careful about customer identity

questions.rationale: Cross-customer contamination is a context-scoping defect, not a window-size problem

questions.question: process_refund fails intermittently because the billing backend times out. What should the tool return so the agent can behave sensibly?

options.A: An empty string
options.C: A structured error with a category and a retryable flag, so the agent can retry or escalate deliberately
options.B: A message asking the user to try later
options.D: The exception stack trace

questions.rationale: Structured errors with categories and retryable flags are what let an agent recover deliberately

questions.question: Which condition should route a ticket to escalate_to_human rather than continue autonomous resolution?

options.A: The customer writes in a language the agent supports
options.D: The request falls outside documented policy, or the agent cannot make progress after a bounded number of attempts
options.B: The order is more than thirty days old
options.C: The conversation exceeds five turns

questions.rationale: Policy gaps and lack of progress are the documented escalation triggers; turn counts and order age are not

questions.question: The agent sometimes calls get_customer when it should call lookup_order. What is the most effective change?

options.B: Reorder the tools in the configuration
options.A: Rewrite both tool descriptions so each states precisely when it applies and how it differs from the other
options.C: Merge them into one tool with a mode flag
options.D: Increase the model's temperature

questions.rationale: Tool selection runs on descriptions, so differentiation is the fix for confusion between similar tools

questions.question: Backend conventions should apply only when backend files are touched. Where do they belong?

options.A: In the root CLAUDE.md so they are always available
options.B: In a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ with frontmatter matching backend paths
options.C: In each engineer's user-level configuration
options.D: In the repository wiki

questions.rationale: Path-scoped rules load conditionally, which is exactly the stated requirement

questions.question: When is plan mode the appropriate choice over direct execution?

options.A: For every change, since planning is always safer
options.C: When the change is large or risky enough that a human should review the approach before edits are made
options.B: Only when the model is unfamiliar with the language
options.D: When the context window is nearly full

questions.rationale: Plan mode is a human review gate for approach, warranted by risk rather than universally

questions.question: A repeated multi-step review procedure should be available to the whole team as a single invocation. What is the right mechanism?

options.A: A shared document describing the steps
options.D: A custom slash command or skill committed to the repository
options.B: A longer CLAUDE.md
options.C: A saved chat transcript

questions.rationale: Repeatable team procedures belong in committed commands or skills, not prose

questions.question: Subagents return full source documents to the coordinator, which then exceeds its context limit. What is the correct design change?

options.B: Give the coordinator a larger model
options.A: Have subagents return structured findings with citations while raw sources stay at the edge or in a scratchpad
options.C: Reduce the number of subagents to one
options.D: Truncate each document to its first page

questions.rationale: Delegation exists to keep bulk at the edge and move distilled results

questions.question: Final reports attribute claims to the wrong sources even though each subagent is individually accurate. What is the likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis model is too small
options.B: The handoff format does not carry claim and source together, so provenance is lost between stages
options.C: The search subagent returns too many results
options.D: Reports are generated before analysis completes

questions.rationale: Provenance survives handoffs only when the format carries claim and source together

questions.question: A subagent fails permanently on one source. What should the coordinator receive?

options.A: Nothing, so the report proceeds
options.C: A propagated error with enough context to decide between retry, exclusion with a noted gap, or abort
options.B: A silent retry loop until it succeeds
options.D: A generic failure flag with no detail

questions.rationale: Errors must propagate with enough context for the coordinator to choose a recovery path

questions.question: The reviewer must emit results a pipeline can parse. Which invocation is correct?

options.A: Interactive session with output redirected to a log
options.D: Non-interactive print mode with JSON output and a schema
options.B: Plan mode with an approval step
options.C: A cron job that emails the transcript

questions.rationale: CI requires non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.question: Reviews flag many low-value style nits and engineers now ignore them. Which change addresses this?

options.B: Post findings to a separate channel
options.A: Define explicit review criteria and a severity bar in the prompt, with examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
options.C: Run the review only on large pull requests
options.D: Cap output at five findings

questions.rationale: Precision comes from explicit criteria and examples that draw the signal boundary

questions.question: Some invoices legitimately lack a delivery date. How should the schema express this?

options.A: Make the field required and let extraction fail
options.B: Make the field nullable so absence is recorded explicitly, with conditional validation where the document type requires it
options.C: Omit the field from the schema
options.D: Default it to today's date

questions.rationale: Nullable fields record legitimate absence; required fields force fabrication or failure

questions.question: Which loop gives the most reliable extraction output?

options.A: Generate, then manually review every record
options.C: Enforce a JSON schema through tool use, validate, and on failure retry with the validation error provided to the model
options.B: Generate three times and take the majority
options.D: Generate with temperature zero and accept the result

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop is the reliability pattern the guide describes

questions.question: Your team reports 97% accuracy measured only on records that passed validation. Why is that number misleading?

options.A: Accuracy should be measured per field, not per record
options.D: It excludes the failures, so it measures where the system already succeeded rather than the true rate across all documents
options.B: 97% is too low to report
options.C: Validation and accuracy are unrelated

questions.rationale: Measuring only validated records is a biased sample; calibration needs coverage of all documents

questions.question: A pipeline has four steps whose order never varies and whose outputs are each checkable. What should it be?

options.A: An agent that plans each run
options.B: Four agents, one per step
options.C: A deterministic workflow with model calls at defined points
options.D: A single prompt covering all four steps

questions.rationale: A known fixed order is encoded rather than rediscovered, which is cheaper and testable per step. Runtime planning (A, B) adds nondeterminism, and one prompt (D) removes the checkpoints

questions.question: What is the principal cost of introducing a subagent?

options.A: It loses the context the parent held unless the handoff carries it explicitly
options.B: It requires a larger model
options.C: It cannot use tools
options.D: It doubles token cost in every case

questions.rationale: Delegation buys isolation and pays in context, which is why handoffs must be explicit. A subagent does not require a larger model (B), can use tools (C), and cost varies with the work (D)

questions.question: An autonomous step would modify production data. What does the architecture require?

options.A: A more capable model
options.B: A longer system prompt describing caution
options.C: A retry policy
options.D: A checkpoint where a person authorises the action, or a reversible mechanism

questions.rationale: Irreversible external effects need an authorisation boundary or reversibility, enforced outside the model. Capability (A), instruction (B), and retries (C) do not bound the consequence

questions.question: What most helps diagnose an agentic failure after the fact?

options.A: The final output alone
options.B: A trace of each step's inputs, tool calls, and outputs
options.C: The total token count
options.D: The model version

questions.rationale: A per-step trace reconstructs a nondeterministic run, which is what diagnosis needs. The final output (A), token totals (C), and version (D) do not show where it diverged

questions.question: Where should repository-wide conventions for Claude Code live?

options.A: In each developer's local configuration
options.B: In a CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
options.C: In the team's chat channel
options.D: In the CI configuration only

questions.rationale: Committed project memory is shared, versioned, and reviewed with the code. Local configuration (A) does not propagate, chat (C) is not read as context, and CI (D) covers automation rather than interactive work

questions.question: Which task is best suited to headless Claude Code in CI?

options.A: Exploratory debugging of an unfamiliar failure
options.B: Designing a new module's architecture
options.C: Pair programming with a developer
options.D: A repeatable, well-specified check that runs on every pull request

questions.rationale: Headless execution suits bounded, repeatable work that runs unattended. Exploration (A), design (B), and pairing (C) all depend on a person in the loop

questions.question: What is a hook for?

options.A: Running a deterministic action at a defined point, independently of the model
options.B: Storing reusable instructions
options.C: Holding project context
options.D: Selecting the model

questions.rationale: Hooks execute as code at fixed points, which is how a guarantee is enforced. Instructions (B) and context (C) belong in project memory, and model choice (D) is configuration

questions.question: A pipeline needs output that always conforms to a fixed shape. What is the correct mechanism?

options.A: Requesting the shape in the prompt and parsing the result
options.B: Post-processing prose with regular expressions
options.C: Declaring the shape as a schema the model must satisfy, and validating on receipt
options.D: Lowering the temperature

questions.rationale: A declared schema makes the shape a contract rather than a request, and validation closes the loop. Prompt requests (A), text parsing (B), and temperature (D) leave the shape to chance

questions.question: How should a schema handle a value the source may not contain?

options.A: Omit the field silently
options.B: Supply a plausible default
options.C: Return an empty string in all cases
options.D: Define an explicit representation for absence

questions.rationale: Absence must be representable so a genuine gap is distinguishable from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, a plausible default (B) fabricates, and an empty string (C) conflates absence with an empty value

questions.question: Extraction succeeds on typical inputs and fails on unusual ones. What is the most effective response?

options.A: Raise the temperature
options.B: Use a larger model
options.C: Add examples covering the unusual formats and state what to return when a field is missing
options.D: Ask the model to be careful with unusual inputs

questions.rationale: The unusual cases fail because they were never specified, and examples plus a missing-value rule specify them. Temperature (A) adds variance, model size (B) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (D) is not specification

questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a tool surface needs redesign rather than better prompting?

options.A: It exposes more than five tools
options.B: The model repeatedly selects a tool that cannot satisfy the request
options.C: The tools are implemented in different services
options.D: The tools return large payloads

questions.rationale: Repeated wrong selection indicates the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (A) and implementation topology (C) are not faults, and payload size (D) is a separate problem

questions.question: How should a tool that deletes records be constrained?

options.A: By enforcing authorisation and scope outside the model
options.B: By a description warning the model to use it carefully
options.C: By requiring more parameters
options.D: By declaring it last among the tools

questions.rationale: Destructive capability is bounded by the surrounding system, since a description is a request rather than a control. Extra parameters (C) and ordering (D) do not limit authority

questions.question: An MCP integration exposes an entire database through one general query tool. What is the architectural concern?

options.A: The model's authority is unbounded, and least privilege cannot be applied
options.B: It will be slow
options.C: It uses too many tokens
options.D: It cannot return structured output

questions.rationale: A single unrestricted tool removes the ability to scope what the model may reach. Speed (B) and tokens (C) are secondary, and structured output (D) is achievable either way

questions.question: Quality degrades steadily through a long agentic run. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The model version changed mid-run
options.B: Accumulated context has diluted the material that matters
options.C: The temperature is too low
options.D: The tools have become slower

questions.rationale: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation. Versions do not change mid-run (A), low temperature (C) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness

questions.question: What must happen for state to survive a compaction boundary?

options.A: Nothing, the model retains what matters
options.B: The context window must be enlarged
options.C: The decisions and constraints that must persist are written into an explicit carried-forward summary
options.D: The run must restart

questions.rationale: Compaction is lossy, so persistence must be deliberate. Relying on recall (A) is unreliable, a larger window (B) only moves the boundary, and restarting (D) discards the work

questions.question: An agentic design calls the same expensive tool repeatedly with identical arguments. What does this indicate?

options.A: Healthy retry behaviour
options.B: The tool is too fast
options.C: The agent is not retaining or reusing the result, which points at the state design
options.D: The model is too capable

questions.rationale: Repeating an identical call means the prior result is not available to the agent, which is a state problem. It is not retry behaviour (A), and neither tool speed (B) nor capability (D) explains it

questions.question: What determines whether two lines of work belong in separate subagents?

options.A: Whether each needs context the other would pollute
options.B: Their combined length
options.C: Whether they use different tools
options.D: Whether they can run in parallel

questions.rationale: Context isolation is the reason subagents exist. Length (B), tool difference (C), and parallelism (D) can all be handled within one context

questions.question: Which design most reduces the cost of a wrong autonomous decision?

options.A: A larger model
options.B: A longer prompt
options.C: More tools
options.D: Making the action reversible, or gating it behind confirmation

questions.rationale: Reversibility and gating bound the consequence, which is what the risk is. Capability (A), prompt length (B), and tools (C) affect the chance of error rather than its cost

questions.question: A CLAUDE.md has grown to several thousand lines. What is the likely effect?

options.A: Better results, because more context is available
options.B: The instructions that matter compete with material that no longer applies
options.C: No effect, since it is read once
options.D: Faster responses

questions.rationale: Project memory is context and dilutes like any other. More is not automatically better (A), it is not free (C), and it does not speed anything up (D)

questions.question: What should be true of a skill before it is committed to a shared repository?

options.A: It is long enough to be useful
options.B: It encodes a procedure the team genuinely repeats, and it is reviewable
options.C: It is written by the most senior engineer
options.D: It covers every edge case

questions.rationale: A shared skill is justified by genuine repetition and must be reviewable like code. Length (A), authorship (C), and exhaustiveness (D) do not establish that

questions.question: Why is committed configuration preferable to per-developer configuration for team conventions?

options.A: It is faster to load
options.B: It uses less context
options.C: It cannot be overridden
options.D: It is versioned, reviewed, and applies to everyone including automation

questions.rationale: Shared, reviewed, versioned context is what makes a convention hold across people and CI. Speed (A) and context size (B) are not the reason, and it can still be overridden locally (C)

questions.question: A schema-validated response fails validation once in every few hundred calls. What is the correct handling?

options.A: Define a fallback path: retry, then fail explicitly rather than passing invalid data on
options.B: Ignore it, since the rate is low
options.C: Disable validation to avoid the failures
options.D: Increase the output token limit

questions.rationale: A rare failure still needs a defined path, and silently passing invalid data is the outcome to prevent. Ignoring it (B) and disabling validation (C) do exactly that, and the token limit (D) is not the cause

questions.question: What is the advantage of validating structured output at the boundary rather than downstream?

options.A: It is cheaper
options.B: It removes the need for a schema
options.C: The failure is caught where it can still be retried or rejected, before it contaminates later steps
options.D: It improves model accuracy

questions.rationale: Catching at the boundary contains the fault. It is not primarily a cost question (A), the schema is what makes it possible (B), and it does not change the model's accuracy (D)

questions.question: A structured extraction must record where in the source each value came from. What does this require?

options.A: A larger model
options.B: A longer prompt
options.C: A second extraction pass
options.D: The schema to include a provenance field the model must populate

questions.rationale: Anything the output must carry has to be part of the declared shape. Model size (A) and prompt length (B) do not create a field, and a second pass (C) is unnecessary if the schema asks for it

questions.question: Two tools do nearly the same thing with different names. What is the architectural fault?

options.A: Duplication of code
options.B: Higher latency
options.C: The model has no reliable basis for choosing between them
options.D: Increased token cost

questions.rationale: Ambiguity at the point of selection is the fault, because the model chooses from descriptions. Code duplication (A), latency (B), and cost (D) are secondary consequences

questions.question: What should a tool do when given arguments it cannot satisfy?

options.A: Return the closest result it can
options.B: Return a clear error stating what was wrong, so the model can correct the call
options.C: Return an empty result
options.D: Raise an exception that terminates the run

questions.rationale: An informative error keeps the model able to adapt. A closest-guess (A) and an empty result (C) are silently wrong, and terminating (D) discards a recoverable run

questions.question: An MCP tool exposes a write operation that the use case never needs. What should happen?

options.A: Remove it, because unused authority is unnecessary risk
options.B: Leave it, since it may be useful later
options.C: Document that it should not be used
options.D: Rename it to discourage use

questions.rationale: Authority that is not needed should not be granted. Retaining it for possible future use (B), documenting (C), or renaming (D) all leave the capability reachable

questions.question: What is the earliest reliable signal that context management has failed in a long run?

options.A: The agent begins repeating work or contradicting earlier decisions
options.B: The run takes longer than expected
options.C: Token cost rises
options.D: A tool returns an error

questions.rationale: Repetition and self-contradiction are the behavioural signature of lost state. Duration (B) and cost (C) rise for many reasons, and a tool error (D) is unrelated

questions.question: Why is a defined success criterion necessary for a reliable agentic system?

options.A: It reduces token cost
options.B: Without it there is no way to tell completion from failure, so the system cannot stop correctly or be measured
options.C: It makes the prompt shorter
options.D: It is required by the platform

questions.rationale: Termination and measurement both depend on a definition of done. Cost (A), prompt length (C), and platform requirements (D) are not the reason

questions.question: A reliability requirement says wrong output must never reach the user unnoticed. What does the design need?

options.A: A more capable model
options.B: More examples in the prompt
options.C: A detection step with a defined action when it fires
options.D: A longer context window

questions.rationale: Preventing silent error requires detection plus a response. Capability (A), examples (B), and context (D) improve the average case without catching the bad one

questions.question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

options.A: Log every update and deletion for later audit
options.D: Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely
options.B: Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
options.C: Restrict deletions to business hours

questions.rationale: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

questions.question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

options.B: The model, which may have degraded overnight
options.A: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
options.C: The system prompt wording
options.D: The temperature setting

questions.rationale: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

questions.question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.A: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
options.B: Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
options.C: One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
options.D: Limit the platform to ten capabilities

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

questions.question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.A: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
options.C: Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
options.B: One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
options.D: A single fine-tuned model for both

questions.rationale: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

questions.question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.A: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
options.D: The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path
options.B: Workflows always outperform agents
options.C: The team lacked time to build an agent

questions.rationale: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

questions.question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

options.B: Ship and count complaints
options.A: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
options.C: Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
options.D: Grade outputs by length

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

questions.question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.A: Roll it out; demos are representative
options.B: Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
options.C: Ask the team to vote
options.D: Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

questions.rationale: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

questions.question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

options.A: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
options.C: A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
options.D: Blocking free-text queries entirely

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

questions.question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

options.A: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
options.D: Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit
options.B: Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
options.C: Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher

questions.rationale: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

questions.question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.B: Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
options.A: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
options.C: Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
options.D: Let each engineer keep personal settings only

questions.rationale: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

questions.question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
options.B: Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
options.C: The Claude API with request logging disabled
options.D: Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit

questions.rationale: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
options.C: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.B: Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
options.D: Let each team choose its own path

questions.rationale: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

questions.question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

options.A: It reduces token cost
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place
options.B: It removes the need for evaluation
options.C: It guarantees lower latency

questions.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

questions.question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

options.B: Force the model to answer within two seconds
options.A: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
options.C: Increase the legacy timeout
options.D: Use the smallest model available

questions.rationale: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

questions.question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

options.A: Using identical prompts in both
options.B: Establishing which behaviours must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
options.C: Choosing the cheaper platform for both
options.D: Deploying to whichever region is nearest

questions.rationale: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behaviour, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

options.A: Which model to use
options.C: Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
options.B: The expected token cost
options.D: Whether the agent can be built in the available time

questions.rationale: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

questions.question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

options.A: The more capable design, since capability is the point
options.D: Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity
options.B: The design the team finds more interesting
options.C: The design with more components, for future flexibility

questions.rationale: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

questions.question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

options.B: Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
options.A: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.C: Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

questions.rationale: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behaviour cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

options.A: It uses more than one model
options.B: Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
options.C: It has an evaluation suite
options.D: It includes a human approval step

questions.rationale: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

questions.question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

options.A: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
options.C: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.B: Agreement from the engineering team
options.D: A completed cost estimate

questions.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

questions.question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

options.A: It gives a reliable measure of quality
options.D: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter
options.B: It is acceptable if it is large enough
options.C: It only matters for regulated systems

questions.rationale: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

questions.question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behaviour. How is this best prevented?

options.B: Changing one thing at a time
options.A: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviours the system must not lose
options.C: Reviewing changes more carefully
options.D: Limiting how often prompts change

questions.rationale: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

questions.question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

options.A: Only a reported incident
options.B: A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
options.C: A fixed annual schedule
options.D: A change in cost

questions.rationale: Any change to the things that determine behaviour invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

options.A: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
