options.C: Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
options.B: Refuse, since logging creates risk
options.D: Log responses only

questions.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

options.A: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
options.D: It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content
options.B: It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
options.C: It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel

questions.rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

questions.question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

options.B: The model provider
options.A: The organisation that deployed the workflow
options.C: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.D: Nobody, since the output was automated

questions.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organisational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

questions.question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

options.A: Provide the headline accuracy figure
options.B: Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
options.C: Explain that quality cannot be summarised
options.D: Provide the model's benchmark score

questions.rationale: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

questions.question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: The cost of additional licences
options.C: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.B: The need for a larger model
options.D: The training schedule

questions.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licences (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

questions.question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

options.A: Full documentation at delivery
options.D: A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update
options.B: A longer warranty period
options.C: Training every user

questions.rationale: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

questions.question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

options.B: One model for everything, for simplicity
options.A: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.C: The largest model for everything, for safety
options.D: The newest model for everything

questions.rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

options.A: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
options.B: A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.C: A limit that only matters for long documents
options.D: A setting to raise when quality drops

questions.rationale: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

questions.question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.A: Appoint one team to own all prompting
options.C: Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
options.B: Freeze the prompts
options.D: Move all prompts into the system prompt

questions.rationale: Prompts that determine production behaviour deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organisation, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

questions.question: An organisation wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

options.A: A written policy circulated by email
options.D: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
options.B: A one-off training session
options.C: Requiring approval for each use

questions.rationale: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

questions.question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement programme is working?

options.B: The number of people trained
options.A: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.C: Licence utilisation
options.D: The volume of tool calls

questions.rationale: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilisation (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

questions.question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

options.A: Whether the team needs more training
options.B: Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
options.C: Whether a larger model would help
options.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

questions.rationale: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

questions.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalogue that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the catalogue nightly
options.C: Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalogue changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
options.B: Load the catalogue into the system prompt
options.D: An autonomous agent that browses the public website

questions.rationale: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

questions.question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

options.A: The generation prompt
options.D: Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently
options.B: The model version
options.C: The user interface

questions.rationale: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

questions.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.B: Shorten all tool descriptions
options.A: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
options.C: Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
options.D: Replace the agent with a larger model

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

questions.question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

options.A: Exact match against reference summaries
options.B: A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
options.C: Average output length compared to references
options.D: User thumbs-up counts alone

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

questions.question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

options.A: Ship it and monitor complaints
options.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
options.B: Team vote followed by rollout
options.D: Rollout with a feedback form

questions.rationale: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

questions.question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

options.A: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
options.D: A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
options.C: Restricting the feature to structured queries only

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

questions.question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

options.B: Review every output regardless of risk
options.A: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
options.C: Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
options.D: Review only what users complain about

questions.rationale: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

questions.question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

options.A: The highest observed number
options.B: Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
options.C: A refusal to quantify
options.D: An average weighted to look favorable

questions.rationale: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

questions.question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

options.A: Response latency targets
options.C: Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
options.B: The choice of programming language
options.D: The number of model providers

questions.rationale: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

questions.question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

options.A: Workflows are always more accurate
options.D: The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable
options.B: Agents cannot process documents
options.C: Workflows use less context

questions.rationale: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

questions.question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

options.B: Splitting the preamble across two requests
options.A: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
options.C: Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
options.D: Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

questions.rationale: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

questions.question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

options.A: The final design only
options.B: The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
options.C: The team members involved
options.D: The implementation timeline

questions.rationale: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

questions.question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

options.A: Final outputs only
options.C: Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
options.B: Aggregate latency metrics only
options.D: User feedback only

questions.rationale: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

questions.question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

options.A: A recorded walkthrough
options.D: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow
options.B: A shared chat channel
options.C: Individual coaching sessions

questions.rationale: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

questions.question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

options.B: Logging modifications for later review
options.A: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
options.C: Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
options.D: Running the agent during business hours only

questions.rationale: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it

questions.question: A client requires that inference run inside their own AWS account. What does this determine?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: That a data processing agreement is sufficient
options.C: Deployment through Amazon Bedrock in the client's account and region
options.D: That request logging must be disabled

questions.rationale: Running inside the client's own cloud boundary is what the requirement describes. A contract (B) and logging settings (D) do not keep the data in the account, and the model family (A) is a separate choice

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud wants identity and audit handled by existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.B: Use the Claude API and rebuild the controls
options.C: Use Bedrock for feature parity
options.D: Let each team decide

questions.rationale: Aligning with the governed platform makes existing controls apply without duplication. Rebuilding (B) drifts, a different cloud (C) creates a second control plane, and per-team choice (D) removes governance

questions.question: What is the main architectural benefit of routing all model traffic through one internal service?

options.A: Lower token prices
options.B: It removes the need for evaluation
options.C: It guarantees lower latency
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are applied consistently in one place

questions.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns are enforced and changed once. It does not change unit price (A), remove evaluation (B), or reduce latency (C)

questions.question: Two designs both satisfy the requirement; one is materially simpler. What decides?

options.A: The more capable design, since headroom is valuable
options.B: Whether any stated requirement needs the extra capability, against the ongoing cost of complexity
options.C: Whichever the team prefers to build
options.D: The one with more components, for flexibility

questions.rationale: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Headroom (A), preference (C), and speculative flexibility (D) pay that cost without justification

questions.question: A required compliance control depends on the model behaving correctly. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Acceptable if measured accuracy is very high
options.B: Not acceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.C: Acceptable with a documented residual risk
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

questions.rationale: A control that must hold needs a guarantee, which probabilistic behaviour cannot supply. High accuracy (A), documentation (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee

questions.question: Where should the boundary of automation be drawn in a solution that makes customer-affecting decisions?

options.A: Wherever the model performs well in testing
options.B: As far as the budget allows
options.C: At whatever the client requests
options.D: Where accountability for the decision sits, keeping those decisions with a person

questions.rationale: Accountability determines what may be automated at all, and that boundary is an architectural decision. Test performance (A), budget (B), and unexamined requests (C) do not address responsibility

questions.question: What must exist before a solution is declared production-ready?

options.A: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.B: A successful demonstration
options.C: Sign-off from the engineering team
options.D: A completed cost model

questions.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar. A demonstration (B), consensus (C), and cost (D) do not establish whether it works

questions.question: An evaluation set contains only cases the system already handles. What is the effect?

options.A: It provides a reliable quality measure
options.B: It is fine if it is large
options.C: It overstates performance and conceals the failures that matter
options.D: It matters only in regulated contexts

questions.rationale: An unrepresentative sample measures the wrong distribution, and size does not correct bias. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix it (B), and the problem is general (D)

questions.question: How should a request to log every prompt and response for audit be handled?

options.A: Implement it, since audit takes precedence
options.B: Decline, because logging creates risk
options.C: Log responses but not prompts
options.D: Establish what the audit requires, because prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data

questions.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real, and the design must serve the audit purpose without retaining more than warranted. Blanket action (A) or refusal (B) ignores one side, and an arbitrary split (C) is unjustified

questions.question: Who is accountable when an automated Claude workflow produces a harmful decision?

options.A: The model provider
options.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.C: The organisation that deployed it
options.D: No one, because the decision was automated

questions.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes. The provider (A) supplies a capability, individual authorship (B) does not transfer organisational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D)

questions.question: A sponsor asks for one number that shows whether the solution is working. What is the right response?

options.A: Give the headline accuracy figure
options.B: Give the measure tied to the decision they face, and state what it does not cover
options.C: Explain that this cannot be reduced to a number
options.D: Give the model's benchmark score

questions.rationale: A useful metric matches the decision and is honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark (D) can mislead, and refusing (C) fails the sponsor

questions.question: A ten-user pilot is about to expand to two thousand users. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.B: Licence cost
options.C: Whether a larger model is needed
options.D: The training rollout plan

questions.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and surfacing those is the architect's contribution. Cost (B), model size (C), and training (D) follow from knowing what breaks

questions.question: How should a model be chosen for a solution containing several distinct tasks?

options.A: Match each task to the smallest model meeting its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.B: One model everywhere, for simplicity
options.C: The largest model everywhere, for safety
options.D: The newest model everywhere

questions.rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate on evidence. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit

questions.question: How should the context window be treated in a production design?

options.A: As capacity to fill as completely as possible
options.B: As a budget allocated deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.C: As a concern only for long documents
options.D: As a setting to increase whenever quality drops

questions.rationale: Context is scarce and its allocation drives quality, so it is designed. Filling it (A) dilutes, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix allocation

questions.question: An organisation wants consistent Claude Code practice across dozens of repositories. What is most durable?

options.A: A policy document circulated once
options.B: A single training session
options.C: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
options.D: Requiring approval for every use

questions.rationale: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (D) adds friction without conveying practice

questions.question: A client will not accept a solution whose behaviour cannot be explained to their auditor. What does this constrain?

options.A: The model family only
options.B: The cost model
options.C: The architecture, which must make decisions traceable and the controls inspectable
options.D: The deployment region

questions.rationale: Auditability is an architectural property covering tracing and inspectable controls. Model family (A), cost (B), and region (D) do not by themselves make behaviour explicable

questions.question: What is the main risk of building directly against a single cloud's model service with no abstraction?

options.A: Moving later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
options.B: Higher token cost
options.C: Lower accuracy
options.D: Slower responses

questions.rationale: Coupling determines the cost of change, which is the architectural concern. Cost (B), accuracy (C), and latency (D) are not consequences of the coupling itself

questions.question: A solution must serve users in two regions with different data residency rules. What follows?

options.A: One deployment in the cheaper region
options.B: A single deployment with encryption in transit
options.C: Whichever region has the lowest latency
options.D: Separate deployments whose data stays within each region's boundary

questions.rationale: Residency is satisfied by keeping the data within each boundary. A single deployment (A, B) moves data across it, and latency (C) does not address the rule

questions.question: A requirement is stated as make it as accurate as possible. What should the architect do?

options.A: Choose the largest model and optimise from there
options.B: Establish the accuracy the use case actually needs and what an error costs
options.C: Build the most complex design the budget allows
options.D: Defer the question until after the pilot

questions.rationale: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be made concrete. Defaulting to maximum capability (A, C) spends without a target, and deferring (D) leaves the design unanchored

questions.question: Two components each work correctly but the system fails intermittently at their boundary. What does this suggest?

options.A: One component needs a larger model
options.B: The contract between them is underspecified, particularly for edge and error cases
options.C: The system needs more components
options.D: The failure is transient and can be retried

questions.rationale: Boundary failures between correct components point at the contract. Capability (A) and more components (C) do not define the interface, and retrying (D) hides it

questions.question: A design proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely. What should the architect raise?

options.A: Nothing, retention is always safer
options.B: That storage is expensive
options.C: That it will slow the system
options.D: Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations retention creates

questions.rationale: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it. Treating retention as free of risk (A) is the error, and cost (B) and speed (C) are minor by comparison

questions.question: How should a solution handle the case where the model is confident and wrong?

options.A: Design so that consequential outputs are verified against something independent of the model
options.B: Trust the confidence signal
options.C: Ask the model to double-check
options.D: Use two models and take the agreement

questions.rationale: Independence is what catches confident error. Confidence (B) is not evidence, self-checking (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D)

questions.question: An evaluation shows 94% accuracy. What else must be known before this is actionable?

options.A: The model version only
options.B: The token cost of the evaluation
options.C: What the 6% look like, and what each failure costs
options.D: How long the evaluation took

questions.rationale: A headline rate is only meaningful alongside the shape and cost of the failures. Version (A), cost (B), and duration (D) do not describe the risk

questions.question: What should happen when a model version is updated beneath a production solution?

options.A: Nothing, versions are compatible
options.B: Increase monitoring for a week
options.C: Roll back automatically if complaints rise
options.D: Re-run the evaluation suite before the change reaches production traffic

questions.rationale: A change to the thing that determines behaviour invalidates prior measurement. Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and monitoring (B) or reacting to complaints (C) detects after users are affected

questions.question: A stakeholder asks why the solution cannot simply be fully automated. What is the most useful answer?

options.A: That the technology is not ready
options.B: That automation is always risky
options.C: Which specific decisions carry accountability or are unverifiable, and what automating them would risk
options.D: That the budget does not allow it

questions.rationale: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited. Generic claims about readiness (A) or risk (B) are not, and budget (D) is not the reason

questions.question: What should be handed over with a solution so it survives its first year?

options.A: The source code
options.B: The evaluation suite, the criteria, the owner, and the routine for re-checking
options.C: A recorded demonstration
options.D: A list of prompts used

questions.rationale: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain, with someone responsible. Code (A), a demonstration (C), and prompts (D) are artefacts without the means to verify them

questions.question: A team reports the solution has become worse, but nothing was deployed. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The inputs or the surrounding usage changed
options.B: The model degraded on its own
options.C: The prompts wore out
options.D: The evaluation was wrong originally

questions.rationale: Behaviour changes with what is fed to it, and distribution drift is the usual cause. Models do not degrade unprompted (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and the original evaluation is not the first suspect (D)

questions.question: How should prompts that determine production behaviour be managed?

options.A: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on change, like code
options.B: Edited in place when someone notices a problem
options.C: Kept in a shared document for easy editing
options.D: Frozen after launch

questions.rationale: Anything that determines production behaviour needs the lifecycle of code. Ad hoc edits (B) and open documents (C) invite unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks improvement

questions.question: An organisation asks how to measure whether Claude Code is worth the licence cost. What should be measured?

options.A: Number of tool invocations
options.B: Change in the delivery outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.C: Number of users onboarded
options.D: Hours spent in the tool

questions.rationale: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated. Invocations (A), onboarding (C), and time in tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit

questions.question: What most often blocks a team from getting good results from Claude Code on an existing codebase?

options.A: The size of the repository
options.B: The programming language
options.C: The absence of committed context describing the conventions and structure
options.D: The number of contributors

questions.rationale: Missing project context is the usual cause, and it is the one the team can fix. Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results
